# Shared schedule showed Fenwick which jobs awaited parts

Fenwick Instrument Repairs trialled a shared bench schedule for six weeks. Manager Priya Vale explains what the team had to settle before it was useful, what the trial did and did not establish, and what would be done differently next time.

By Thomas Barregren

Jobs waiting for parts and jobs ready for work used to appear on separate paper sheets at Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments. In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, choosing Benchline after checking that it could tell those two statuses apart. Workshop manager Priya Vale has since approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog.

## ‘Ready for work’ needed an agreed meaning

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session, while collection arrangements stayed on the telephone.

Asked in an email interview what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale wrote: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The trial recorded visibility rather than faster repairs

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule and says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

What the trial establishes is the team’s reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed.

## An extra week before the backlog goes in

Asked whether the team would make the same choice again, and what would change, Vale replied: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

A workshop weighing a similar trial can start where Fenwick did: agree what each status means and who updates it, and leave time to check those names before older jobs are added.
EOF

# Shared schedule showed Fenwick which jobs awaited parts

Fenwick Instrument Repairs trialled a shared bench schedule for six weeks. Manager Priya Vale explains what the team had to settle before it was useful, what the trial did and did not establish, and what would be done differently next time.

By Thomas Barregren

Jobs waiting for parts and jobs ready for work used to appear on separate paper sheets at Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments. In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, choosing Benchline after checking that it could tell those two statuses apart. Workshop manager Priya Vale has since approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog.

## ‘Ready for work’ needed an agreed meaning

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session, while collection arrangements stayed on the telephone.

Asked in an email interview what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale wrote: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The trial recorded visibility rather than faster repairs

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule and says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

What the trial establishes is the team’s reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed.

## An extra week before the backlog goes in

Asked whether the team would make the same choice again, and what would change, Vale replied: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

A workshop weighing a similar trial can start where Fenwick did: agree what each status means and who updates it, and leave time to check those names before older jobs are added.

**A3. Standfirst (l.3).** "Manager Priya Vale explains what the team had to settle before it was useful, what the trial did and did not establish, and what would be done differently."
